title: Hamas Agrees to Gaza Disarmament Framework but Demands Israel Act First
excerpt: Trump hails the Board of Peace deal as a milestone, but a standoff over sequencing — who disarms and who withdraws first — threatens to stall implementation.
body:
• Hamas has agreed to a broad framework for disarming in Gaza, brokered by Trump's Board of Peace, marking the first time the group has accepted a disarmament plan in principle
  • The 15-point road map envisions phased weapons handover, tunnel destruction, and full Israeli withdrawal over approximately 250 days
  • Hamas insists Israel must first end attacks and withdraw forces under a prior agreement before implementation begins
  • Israel says it will not pull back until Hamas is disarmed, creating a standoff that could delay reconstruction

Hamas has agreed to a comprehensive framework for disarming in Gaza, U.S. President Donald Trump announced Thursday, calling it a "major milestone" in ending the conflict. But the deal immediately hit a wall over sequencing, with Hamas and Israel each demanding the other act first.

The agreement, brokered by Trump's Board of Peace under chief envoy Nickolay Mladenov, outlines a 15-point road map for the complete disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups in the Gaza Strip, according to the Wall Street Journal.

What the Deal Contains

The road map envisions a phased process spanning roughly 250 days. In the initial 15-day phase, the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) — the technocratic body set up to govern the enclave — would take security and administrative control and begin preparations for weapons collection.

Subsequent phases call for Israel to remove heavy weapons from areas under its control, Hamas to surrender heavy weaponry and permit the destruction of all tunnels and military infrastructure, and the NCAG's security forces to collect and register all remaining firearms, including an estimated 60,000 rifles.

The final phase involves independent verification and a complete Israeli withdrawal from Gaza, except for a yet-to-be-defined security perimeter.

The Sequencing Standoff

Senior Hamas official Ghazi Hamad told Reuters the agreement was a "comprehensive framework" extending beyond disarmament alone, contingent on Israel first fulfilling commitments under a prior deal struck in Sharm el-Sheikh.

"We insisted to the mediators that Israel must abide by the agreement."

— Ghazi Hamad, Senior Hamas Official

Under that earlier agreement, Hamad said, Israel is obligated to end attacks in Gaza, withdraw forces to their October positions, and increase the flow of goods and humanitarian aid.

An Israeli official responded that Israel would not agree to withdraw behind the so-called Yellow Line — which divides Gaza between Israeli and Hamas-controlled areas — before Hamas is fully disarmed and the Strip demilitarized.

A Reversal from Previous Rejection

The agreement marks a significant shift for Hamas, which publicly rejected calls to disarm as recently as April. At that time, the group refused the Board of Peace's phased disarmament plan, accusing Mladenov of bias toward Israel and demanding a full Israeli withdrawal before any discussions on weapons.

Egypt, which is hosting the talks, noted the parties' "agreement to the road map" and announced a future meeting in Cairo "to discuss implementation mechanisms," though it did not explicitly mention disarmament in its statement.

Stakes for Gaza's Population

The outcome carries enormous consequences for Gaza's roughly two million residents. Israel's military response to Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack has left about 70,000 Palestinians dead, according to Gaza's health ministry, displaced an estimated 90% of the population, and reduced large swaths of the territory to rubble.

Reconstruction is contingent on the disarmament process moving forward. If negotiations stall, millions will remain in tents without the ability to rebuild homes or resume normal life.

For Indians and the broader diaspora monitoring the situation, the Gaza framework has implications for regional stability, energy markets, and the safety of Indian workers across the Middle East.
